title: Shakshuka
subtitle: Eggs poached in spiced tomato sauce
excerpt: Shakshuka is eggs poached directly in a rich spiced tomato and pepper sauce. It is eaten for breakfast, lunch, and dinner across the Middle East and North Africa. The sauce comes together in under 20 minutes. Serve straight from the pan with bread to mop up the sauce.
sourceNotes: Shakshuka is claimed by several countries including Tunisia, Libya, and Israel, where it was brought by Maghrebi Jewish immigrants in the mid-20th century. The word derives from an Arabic root meaning a mixture or all shaken together.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: The tomato sauce can be made 3 days ahead. Add and poach the eggs just before serving.

content.text: Use a wide pan with a lid so you can cover the eggs as they cook. The yolks should be just set but still soft -- check at 5 minutes. If you like runny yolks, check at 4 minutes.
Heat the oil in a wide frying pan over medium heat. Add the onion and cook for 7 minutes until soft.
Add the garlic, peppers, and chilli flakes. Cook for 5 minutes until the peppers soften.
Add the cumin and paprika. Stir for 1 minute. Add the tinned tomatoes and salt. Stir well.
Cook the sauce uncovered for 8 minutes, stirring occasionally, until it thickens.
Use a spoon to make 6 wells in the sauce. Crack an egg into each well.
Cover the pan and cook over low heat for 5 to 6 minutes until the whites are just set and the yolks are still soft. Serve straight from the pan with crusty bread.

items.symptom: Egg whites are still clear while yolks have set
items.cause: Heat is too high -- the yolks cook before the whites can firm up
items.fix: Keep the heat low and make sure the lid is on so steam finishes the whites gently
Cook the sauce for another 5 minutes before adding the eggs
Cook with the lid on for 2 more minutes; check from the edge of the pan where eggs cook fastest

content.text: Shakshuka is eaten across the Middle East and North Africa, and has become one of the most popular dishes in Israel. It is served at breakfast in Tunisia with harissa, for brunch in Tel Aviv with feta, and for dinner across Egypt and Libya. The pan goes straight to the table and everyone eats from it.
